w4-q1: Incorrect — humidity is measured by a humidity sensor, not by an ultrasonic sensor.
Correct — the ultrasonic sensor measures the distance at which the detected object is located in the AID system.
Incorrect — soil pH needs a chemical or soil sensor; ultrasonic sensors work with sound-wave echoes.
Incorrect — light intensity is measured by a photodetector or LDR, not by an ultrasonic sensor.
w4-q2: Incorrect — a camera is a sensing device that captures images; it does not process the data from other sensors.
Incorrect — an NFC tag is a passive short-range storage and identification element, not a processing unit.
Correct — the microcontroller processes the data received from the sensors in the AID system.
Incorrect — the ultrasonic sensor is itself a data source that measures distance, not the component that processes data.
w4-q3: Correct — nanodevices can communicate using electromagnetic communication, as discussed in the lecture.
Correct — nanodevices can also communicate using molecular communication, as discussed in the lecture.
Incorrect — wired Ethernet needs cables and large connectors, which are impractical for nanoscale devices.
Incorrect — ZigBee is a conventional short-range radio standard meant for ordinary devices, not the nanodevice approach discussed.
w4-q4: Correct — sensing coverage guarantees connectivity when the transmission range is at least twice the sensing range.
Incorrect — the condition is the other way round: it is the transmission range that must be at least twice the sensing range.
Incorrect — equal ranges are not enough; the transmission range must be at least twice the sensing range.
Incorrect — a transmission range smaller than the sensing range makes connectivity even less likely to be guaranteed.
w4-q5: Correct — area coverage is a standard coverage problem in a static wireless sensor network.
Incorrect — data compression is a data-handling task, not a coverage category.
Incorrect — route encryption is a security task, not a coverage category.
Incorrect — clock synchronization is a networking task, not a coverage category.
w4-q6: Correct — forest-fire monitoring uses event-driven reporting, where nodes report data when a fire-related event is detected.
Incorrect — on-demand reporting is used when data is requested, such as in an inventory-control system, not for fire detection.
Incorrect — manual reporting involves human effort and is unsuitable for automatic, timely fire detection.
Incorrect — location-based reporting is not the reporting method identified for forest-fire monitoring.
w4-q7: Incorrect — a data mule does not replace sensor nodes; the nodes still sense the data.
Incorrect — a data mule does not measure anything; it collects data from sensor nodes and carries it to the sink.
Correct — a data mule visits sensor nodes, collects their data, and delivers it to the sink.
Incorrect — repairing hardware is a maintenance job, not the role of a data mule.
w4-q8: Correct — failure of a critical stationary node may divide the network into disconnected parts, partitioning it.
Incorrect — stationary nodes stay fixed, so a failure does not make all nodes mobile.
Incorrect — a node failure does not change the sensing range, and certainly does not double it.
Incorrect — stationary nodes cannot move, so the network cannot repair itself by movement.
w4-q9: Incorrect — a router forwards packets between networks, which is not what a person providing sensing information does.
Incorrect — a radio channel is the wireless medium for transmission, not a role a person plays.
Incorrect — an actuator performs physical actions; a person providing information is not acting as one here.
Correct — in human-centric sensing, a person may act as a data source by providing or collecting information.
w4-q10: Correct — in a stationary WSN nodes remain fixed, so deployment and topology maintenance are comparatively easier.
Incorrect — stationary nodes cannot move automatically after a failure, so this is not a feature of such a network.
Incorrect — a continuously changing topology is typical of mobile networks, not stationary ones.
Incorrect — nodes in a stationary WSN remain fixed, so unpredictable sensor locations are not an advantage of such a network.
w4-q11: Correct — UAVs are mobile, so their relative positions and links change often, making the topology change frequently.
Incorrect — the statement is true; UAV movement does cause frequent topology changes, so calling it false is wrong.
w4-q12: Correct — UAV movement causes frequent changes in network topology and communication links, a common issue.
Incorrect — UAVs move, so their relative positions are not fixed.
Incorrect — links between moving UAVs are not permanent, as they change with position.
Incorrect — UAVs can fail, so assuming no possibility of failure is unrealistic.
w4-q13: Incorrect — traditional SCADA commonly uses isolated proprietary systems, whereas M2M is not restricted to isolated systems.
Incorrect — M2M is about devices communicating with each other, so saying it supports no device communication is wrong.
Incorrect — M2M allows devices to exchange data automatically, without continuous human control.
Correct — M2M supports cross-platform integration, unlike traditional SCADA with its isolated proprietary systems.
w4-q14: Incorrect — the statement is true only if nodes could move, but nodes in a stationary WSN remain fixed.
Correct — sensor nodes in a stationary WSN remain fixed, so they cannot move automatically to repair connectivity.
w4-q15: Correct — M2M allows machines or devices to exchange data automatically, without direct human control.
Incorrect — M2M is automatic data exchange, so it does not require every exchange to be manual.
Incorrect — many devices can communicate in an M2M network, not just one at a time.
Incorrect — M2M devices do communicate through a network.
